name: Sirius
workload: TPC-H benchmark (22 queries) hot runs at scale factors SF100/300/500/1000 (100GB-1TB), Sirius (a GPU execution engine plugged into DuckDB via Substrait) vs plain DuckDB on CPU
claimed_speedup: 5.5x faster at SF100 (1.71s vs 9.37s), 5.7x at SF300 (4.48s vs 25.72s), 5.2x at SF500 (8.14s vs 42.25s), 2.7x at SF1000 (31.79s vs 85.91s); also 2.1x-5.3x cheaper per run
benchmark_url: https://github.com/sirius-db/sirius (README performance chart; image at docs/super-sirius-perf.png)
hardware: Sirius (GPU): AWS g7e.2xl/4xl/8xl instances, NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 96GB; DuckDB (CPU) v1.5.5: AWS Graviton5 m9g.16xlarge
tradeoffs: Requires an NVIDIA GPU (Turing+, CUDA 12.x/13.x) and Linux with io_uring enabled; plugs into DuckDB via Substrait and falls back silently to CPU for unsupported operators; only DuckDB is a supported target today (StarRocks integration planned)
caveats: First-party benchmark; numbers were read from a bar chart PNG in the README, not a raw results table; no compiler/build flags stated; the speedup margin shrinks as scale grows (5.5x at SF100 down to 2.7x at SF1000), suggesting GPU memory/bandwidth becomes the bottleneck at larger sizes
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "sirius GPU DuckDB"; gh api repos/sirius-db/sirius

name: cuDF (cudf.pandas)
workload: H2O.ai/DuckDB 'database-like ops' benchmark (join and groupby operations) on a ~5GB dataset, pandas vs cudf.pandas zero-code-change GPU accelerator
claimed_speedup: up to 150x faster (workload dropped from minutes to 1-2 seconds)
hardware: NVIDIA Grace Hopper (GH200) GPU; Intel Xeon Platinum 8480C CPU for the pandas baseline; pandas 2.2, RAPIDS cuDF 23.10
tradeoffs: Requires an NVIDIA GPU; cudf.pandas silently falls back to CPU pandas for unsupported operations, so realized speedup on arbitrary code varies widely from the headline figure
caveats: Benchmark run and published by NVIDIA (vendor), not an independent third party, though it uses the public H2O.ai/DuckDB database-like-ops benchmark suite; compiler/build flags not stated (not a natural fit for this GPU/Python stack)
found_via: GitHub: gh api repos/rapidsai/cudf; NVIDIA developer blog

name: Umbra
workload: ClickBench: 43 analytical SQL queries over the ~100M-row 'hits' web-analytics table, single-node AWS c6a.4xlarge
claimed_speedup: sum of best-of-3 times across all 43 ClickBench queries: 7.41s for Umbra vs 18.03s for ClickHouse (~2.4x faster) and vs 26.25s for DuckDB (~3.5x faster), with 0 failed queries (derived from page data)
stars_or_usage: consistently one of the top single-node finishers on ClickBench; commercial spin-off is CedarDB
tradeoffs: Closed-source (research prototype from TU Munich, now commercialized); distributed only as a prebuilt Docker image (umbradb/umbra); PostgreSQL wire-compatible
caveats: No public source code; run through ClickBench's standardized harness using the vendor's prebuilt, versioned Docker image, so compiler/build flags are not stated/applicable; ClickBench's own README cautions that comparisons across very different system architectures are not perfectly apples-to-apples

name: Velox
workload: ClickBench: 43 analytical SQL queries over the ~100M-row 'hits' table (single Parquet file, queried in place), single-node AWS c6a.xlarge, driven through Meta's Axiom SQL layer on top of the Velox execution engine
claimed_speedup: best case ~2.3x faster than ClickHouse on one query (Q33: 10.49s vs 17.57s) and 1.5-1.8x faster on three others, but slower overall: sum of best-of-3 times across all 43 queries is 214.09s for Velox/Axiom vs 124.35s for ClickHouse, and far slower (>100x) on several count-style queries (derived from page data)
compiler_and_flags: CMake Release build on Ubuntu 24.04 with default toolchain (-DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release); no explicit compiler name/version or optimization flags beyond that stated
tradeoffs: Velox itself is only a C++ execution-engine library with no SQL parser/optimizer/catalog; this result actually benchmarks facebookincubator/axiom (a thin SQL layer built on Velox); must be built from source (no release binaries), which is memory- and time-intensive
caveats: Mixed/weak result: wins on a handful of queries by 1.5-2.3x but is ~1.7x slower in aggregate and drastically slower on several queries; ClickBench's own README is openly hostile to the Velox paper ('a dishonest academic paper'); included here for the documented per-query wins, not as an overall 'faster than ClickHouse' claim

name: Bodo DataFrames
language: Python (JIT-compiled to native code via an MPI-based C++ runtime)
workload: NYC Taxi FHVHV benchmark: 1.03B-row / 24-column Parquet dataset (24.7 GiB) joined with a small weather CSV, average-trip-duration/count aggregation; single-node run on one AWS r6i.16xlarge (32 physical cores, 512 GiB RAM)
claimed_speedup: single node: Bodo 27.71s vs Polars 1.25.2 at 282.34s (~10.2x faster) and vs Daft 0.4.7 at 69.59s (~2.5x faster); 4-node cluster: Bodo 17s vs PySpark 3.5.2 at 389s (20x), Dask at 915s (50x), Modin+Ray at 4155s (250x) (derived from page data)
hardware: AWS EC2 r6i.16xlarge (32 physical cores, 512 GiB RAM); cluster variant uses 4x r6i.16xlarge
tradeoffs: Drop-in pandas-API replacement but relies on JIT compilation and MPI for parallelism; the Bodo Platform build used for the cluster run links a forked version of Arrow for faster Parquet reads (bodo-ai/arrow-cpp-feedstock), a deviation from stock Apache Arrow
caveats: First-party benchmark (Bodo's own repo), not an independent suite; numbers are read from bar-chart PNGs rather than a raw results table; single-node comparison excludes pandas directly (pandas cannot practically process this dataset on one machine); results are dated snapshots (Dec 2024 / Mar 2025) of specific package versions
found_via: GitHub: gh api repos/bodo-ai/bodo (README benchmarks section)

name: chDB
workload: ClickBench 'DataFrame' comparison view (43 analytical queries over the hits dataset), chDB vs Pandas vs Polars vs DuckDB, all run in DataFrame mode on AWS c6a.metal (500GB gp2)
claimed_speedup: aggregate relative time across all queries: chDB 1.35x vs Pandas 71.18x and Polars 9.99x (best-per-query = 1.00x) -> chDB is roughly 53x faster than Pandas and 7.4x faster than Polars in this comparison, and about on par with DuckDB (1.35x vs 1.40x) (derived from page data)
benchmark_url: https://github.com/chdb-io/chdb/raw/main/docs/_static/df_bench.png (image embedded in the chDB README, sourced from the live benchmark.clickhouse.com DataFrame comparison)
tradeoffs: chDB embeds ClickHouse's own vectorized engine as an in-process library (no server, no network round-trip), so the win over Pandas/Polars mainly reflects ClickHouse's engine rather than a new algorithm; heavier binary/startup footprint than a pure-Python library
caveats: Numbers read from a screenshot table embedded in the README, generated from the live, JS-rendered benchmark.clickhouse.com page (which this session could not render directly); the 'beats DuckDB' part of the claim (1.35x vs 1.40x) is marginal/within noise, unlike the large, clear wins over Pandas and Polars
found_via: GitHub: gh api repos/chdb-io/chdb (README Benchmark section)
